questions.stem_html:
A 25-year-old woman has photosensitive facial erythema, oral ulcers, inflammatory hand pain, and edema. Urinalysis shows protein and red-cell casts. Antinuclear and anti-double-stranded DNA antibodies are positive, and serum C3 and C4 are low. Kidney biopsy shows granular capillary-wall and mesangial immunofluorescence.

Which immune mechanism best explains the renal lesion?

options.text_html: Deposition of circulating antigen-antibody complexes with complement activation
Antibody binding directly to a fixed basement-membrane antigen in a linear pattern
Cytotoxic T-cell destruction of glomerular podocytes without antibody participation
IgE-mediated mast-cell degranulation within glomerular capillaries
Loss of peripheral tolerance restricted to red-cell membrane antigens

questions.explanation_html: Nuclear antigens form circulating immune complexes that deposit in glomeruli and activate complement. Consumption lowers serum C3/C4, and granular immunofluorescence reflects deposited complexes. The multisystem disease, anti-dsDNA antibodies, low complement, and granular deposits are classic for type III immune-complex injury.

wrong_choice_explanations.2: Direct anti-basement-membrane disease produces linear immunofluorescence rather than granular lupus deposits.
wrong_choice_explanations.3: SLE nephritis is primarily immune-complex mediated, not isolated T-cell podocyte cytotoxicity.
wrong_choice_explanations.4: Type I hypersensitivity does not produce immune-complex nephritis with low complement.
wrong_choice_explanations.5: SLE can cause hemolysis, but restriction to red-cell antigens would not explain nephritis and granular deposits.

questions.educational_objective: Recognize lupus nephritis as a type III hypersensitivity process characterized by immune-complex deposition, complement activation, and granular immunofluorescence.
